why: Stopping regular coffee causes tiredness and drowsiness within 1-2 days; this is the most reliable caffeine-withdrawal symptom.
source: Juliano & Griffiths 2004, Psychopharmacology 176:1-29 (review of caffeine withdrawal)

why: THC raises anxiety and paranoid thinking on average, and a crowded unfamiliar setting makes this more likely rather than relaxing.
source: D'Souza et al. 2004 Neuropsychopharmacology 29:1558; Freeman et al. 2015 Schizophr Bull 41:391

why: Evening alcohol fragments the second half of sleep and suppresses REM, so people feel less rested the next morning even after moderate drinking.
source: Ebrahim et al. 2013 Alcohol Clin Exp Res 37:539 (review of alcohol and sleep)

why: In healthy people without ADHD, methylphenidate gives only small gains in attention and working memory, smaller than people expect.
source: Ilieva, Hook & Farah 2015 J Cogn Neurosci 27:1069 (meta-analysis)

why: In ADHD, methylphenidate reliably improves sustained attention, with moderate to large effect sizes in trials.
source: Cortese et al. 2018 Lancet Psychiatry 5:727 (network meta-analysis)

why: A single session of moderate-vigorous exercise lowers state anxiety for a few hours afterwards.
source: Petruzzello et al. 1991 Sports Med 11:143; Ensari et al. 2015 Depress Anxiety 32:624 (meta-analyses)

why: MDMA's signature effect is strong feelings of closeness, trust and openness to others.
source: Kirkpatrick et al. 2014 Neuropsychopharmacology 39:1654; Hysek et al. 2014 Soc Cogn Affect Neurosci 9:1645

why: Benzodiazepines such as diazepam reduce anxiety quickly and clearly in generalised anxiety disorder.
source: Baldwin et al. 2014 J Psychopharmacol 28:403 (BAP guidelines); Gomez et al. 2018 Expert Opin Pharmacother 19:883

why: A 5 mg oral dose of diazepam alone has negligible effect on breathing in a healthy adult; the danger comes from combining it with opioids or alcohol.
source: Dahan et al. 2010 Anesthesiology 112:226 context; FDA 2016 boxed warning on benzodiazepine-opioid combination

why: After several weeks, SSRIs lift mood in major depression, though the average advantage is modest.
source: Cipriani et al. 2018 Lancet 391:1357 (network meta-analysis of 21 antidepressants)

why: A single SSRI dose does not make a healthy person feel happier; antidepressant effects take weeks.
source: Harmer et al. 2009 Br J Psychiatry 195:102; Harmer, Duman & Cowen 2017 Lancet Psychiatry 4:409

why: 25 mg CBD is well below the 300-600 mg oral doses that reduced anxiety in lab studies, and low doses performed like placebo.
source: Zuardi et al. 2017 Front Pharmacol 8:259 (inverted-U dose curve); Linares et al. 2019 Braz J Psychiatry 41:9

why: CBD is not intoxicating and does not alter perception.
source: WHO Expert Committee on Drug Dependence 2018, Cannabidiol critical review

why: Quitting smoking brings irritability, restlessness and anxiety within the first days.
source: Hughes 2007 Nicotine Tob Res 9:315 (review of tobacco withdrawal); DSM-5 tobacco withdrawal criteria

why: Increased appetite is a standard nicotine-withdrawal symptom and drives post-quitting weight gain.
source: Hughes 2007 Nicotine Tob Res 9:315; DSM-5 tobacco withdrawal criteria

why: Two drinks reduce tension and anxiety modestly while blood alcohol is rising.
source: Sher & Levenson 1982 J Abnorm Psychol 91:350; Bresin et al. 2018 Psychol Bull 144:1036 (meta-analysis)

why: 10 mg oral morphine gives clear pain relief in experimental and clinical pain.
source: Moore & McQuay 1997 Pain (Oxford league table of analgesics); Staahl et al. 2009 Pain 146:116

why: A normal oral morphine dose measurably lowers breathing drive in a non-tolerant person, but not dangerously when taken alone.
source: Dahan, Aarts & Smith 2010 Anesthesiology 112:226 (opioid-induced respiratory depression review)

why: Injected or smoked heroin reaches the brain fast and clearly suppresses breathing, which is how overdose kills.
source: Pattinson 2008 Br J Anaesth 100:747; White & Irvine 1999 Addiction 94:961

why: During a sub-anaesthetic infusion ketamine causes strong dissociation and changed perception.
source: Krystal et al. 1994 Arch Gen Psychiatry 51:199; Murrough et al. 2013 Am J Psychiatry 170:1134

why: In major depression, one ketamine infusion lifts mood within a day, after the dissociation has worn off.
source: Zarate et al. 2006 Arch Gen Psychiatry 63:856; Newport et al. 2015 Am J Psychiatry 172:950 (meta-analysis)

why: A 15-25 mg psilocybin dose produces strong visual and perceptual changes at peak.
source: Griffiths et al. 2006 Psychopharmacology 187:268; Hirschfeld & Schmidt 2021 J Psychopharmacol 35:384 (dose-response meta-analysis)

why: A small haloperidol dose in healthy people causes sedation and lower alertness rather than anything pleasant.
source: King 1997 J Psychopharmacol 11:99 (review of neuroleptics in healthy volunteers); Ramaekers et al. 1999 Neuropsychopharmacology 21:775

why: A single 40 mg propranolol dose leaves mood essentially unchanged in healthy people.
source: Steenen et al. 2016 J Psychopharmacol 30:128 (systematic review of propranolol for anxiety)

why: Low-dose melatonin taken in the evening modestly increases sleepiness and shortens time to fall asleep by several minutes.
source: Ferracioli-Oda et al. 2013 PLoS One 8:e63773 (meta-analysis); Zhdanova et al. 1995 Clin Pharmacol Ther 57:552

why: Weekly semaglutide clearly lowers hunger and food cravings, cutting energy intake by about a quarter.
source: Blundell et al. 2017 Diabetes Obes Metab 19:1242; Friedrichsen et al. 2021 Diabetes Obes Metab 23:754

why: Methamphetamine strongly suppresses appetite.
source: Hart et al. 2001 Psychopharmacology 159:397; Cruickshank & Dyer 2009 Addiction 104:1085

why: Smoked THC increases appetite and food intake (the 'munchies').
source: Foltin et al. 1988 Appetite 11:1; Kirkham 2009 Int Rev Psychiatry 21:163

why: Warm time with friends and touch increases felt connection and trust.
source: Holt-Lunstad et al. 2008 Psychosom Med 70:976; Dunbar 2010 Neurosci Biobehav Rev 34:260

why: After only 4 hours of sleep people feel clearly sleepier the next day.
source: Van Dongen et al. 2003 Sleep 26:117; Lim & Dinges 2010 Psychol Bull 136:375

why: Stimulants improve attention much more in people with ADHD than in healthy people, who start near their ceiling.
source: Cortese et al. 2018 Lancet Psychiatry 5:727; Ilieva et al. 2015 J Cogn Neurosci 27:1069

why: Daily coffee drinkers build tolerance, so a cup mostly brings them back to normal rather than above a non-user.
source: James & Rogers 2005 Psychopharmacology 182:1; Rogers et al. 2010 Neuropsychopharmacology 35:1973

why: Alcohol adds to the breathing suppression from opioids, and the combination is present in many overdose deaths.
source: van der Schrier et al. 2017 Anesthesiology 126:534; Darke & Zador 1996 Addiction 91:405

why: Naloxone pushes heroin off opioid receptors and quickly restores breathing.
source: Boyer 2012 N Engl J Med 367:146 (management of opioid analgesic overdose); WHO 2014 community management of opioid overdose

why: THC intoxication and perceptual change increase with dose.
source: Hollister 1986 Pharmacol Rev 38:1; Curran et al. 2002 Psychopharmacology 164:61

why: Attention and reaction time get worse as blood alcohol rises.
source: Zoethout et al. 2011 J Psychopharmacol 25:1563 (review of alcohol dose and CNS performance)

why: Tolerance to the pain-relieving effect of opioids builds with daily use, so the same dose works less well.
source: Chu et al. 2006 J Pain 7:43; Morgan & Christie 2011 Br J Pharmacol 164:1322

why: One coffee barely changes anxiety, but around 400 mg at once reliably causes jitteriness and nervousness.
source: Smith 2002 Food Chem Toxicol 40:1243; Childs et al. 2008 Neuropsychopharmacology 33:2791

why: Diazepam is a proven anti-anxiety drug; theanine's calming effect is small and inconsistent at best.
source: Baldwin et al. 2014 J Psychopharmacol 28:403; Williams et al. 2020 Plant Foods Hum Nutr 75:12 (theanine systematic review)

why: Many autistic people have higher sensory sensitivity, so loud, bright, crowded places are more distressing for them.
source: Green & Ben-Sasson 2010 J Autism Dev Disord 40:1495; Robertson & Baron-Cohen 2017 Nat Rev Neurosci 18:671

why: A psilocybin trip starts within about an hour, peaks at 1.5-2.5 hours and is mostly over by about 6 hours.
source: Hasler et al. 2004 Psychopharmacology 172:145; Brown et al. 2017 Clin Pharmacokinet 56:1543; Holze et al. 2023 Clin Pharmacol Ther 113:822

why: An LSD trip lasts much longer than psilocybin: peak after a few hours and effects for about 8-12 hours.
source: Dolder et al. 2017 Clin Pharmacokinet 56:1219; Holze et al. 2021 Neuropsychopharmacology 46:537

why: Snorted cocaine works within minutes, peaks around 20-40 minutes and fades within about an hour or two.
source: Javaid et al. 1978 Science 202:227; Van Dyke et al. 1978 Science 200:211

why: Caffeine peaks in the blood 30-60 minutes after a coffee and has a half-life of about 5 hours, so the lift fades over the afternoon.
source: Fredholm et al. 1999 Pharmacol Rev 51:83; Institute of Medicine 2001 Caffeine for the Sustainment of Mental Task Performance

why: MDMA effects begin within about 45 minutes, peak at around 1.5-2 hours and last about 4-6 hours.
source: Hysek et al. 2012 J Pharmacol Exp Ther 340:286; Vizeli & Liechti 2017 J Psychopharmacol 31:576

why: Immediate-release Ritalin works within about 30-60 minutes and lasts about 3-4 hours.
source: Swanson et al. 1999 Clin Pharmacol Ther 66:295; Kimko et al. 1999 Clin Pharmacokinet 37:457

why: Dissociation from a 40-minute ketamine infusion builds during the infusion and is largely gone within an hour of its end.
source: Murrough et al. 2013 Am J Psychiatry 170:1134; Luckenbaugh et al. 2014 J Affect Disord 159:56

why: Smoked cannabis acts within minutes, peaks within the first half hour to an hour and wears off over 2-4 hours.
source: Grotenhermen 2003 Clin Pharmacokinet 42:327; Huestis 2007 Chem Biodivers 4:1770

why: Oral immediate-release morphine starts working within about 30 minutes, peaks at about 1 hour and lasts about 4 hours.
source: Lugo & Kern 2002 J Pain Palliat Care Pharmacother 16:5; BNF morphine monograph

why: The pleasant lift from two drinks follows rising blood alcohol, peaking within the first hour and fading as levels fall.
source: King et al. 2011 Arch Gen Psychiatry 68:389; Martin et al. 1993 Alcohol Clin Exp Res 17:140 (biphasic alcohol effects)

why: Cocaine blocks the dopamine transporter, raising striatal dopamine several-fold in microdialysis and clearly in human PET.
source: Volkow et al. 1997 Nature 386:827; Di Chiara & Imperato 1988 PNAS 85:5274; Cox et al. 2009 J Neurosci 29:12957

why: Caffeine blocks adenosine receptors rather than lowering adenosine itself, so adenosine levels stay about the same.
source: Fredholm et al. 1999 Pharmacol Rev 51:83; Porkka-Heiskanen et al. 1997 Science 276:1265

why: A social-evaluative stressor raises blood cortisol, peaking about 20-40 minutes after it starts.
source: Dickerson & Kemeny 2004 Psychol Bull 130:355 (meta-analysis); Kirschbaum et al. 1993 Neuropsychobiology 28:76

why: ACTH rises faster and more steeply than cortisol during an acute psychological stressor.
source: Kirschbaum et al. 1993 Neuropsychobiology 28:76; Foley & Kirschbaum 2010 Neurosci Biobehav Rev 35:91

why: Ghrelin, the hunger hormone, drops after a meal and rises again before the next one.
source: Cummings et al. 2001 Diabetes 50:1714; Callahan et al. 2004 J Clin Endocrinol Metab 89:1319

why: GLP-1 is released from the gut within minutes of eating.
source: Holst 2007 Physiol Rev 87:1409; Orskov et al. 1996 Scand J Gastroenterol 31:665

why: MDMA clearly raises blood oxytocin in humans, which is thought to contribute to its social effects.
source: Dumont et al. 2009 J Psychopharmacol 23:681; Hysek et al. 2014 Soc Cogn Affect Neurosci 9:1645

why: Even 0.5-1 mg of oral melatonin taken in the daytime raises blood melatonin far above its very low daytime level.
source: Dollins et al. 1994 PNAS 91:1824; Zhdanova et al. 1995 Clin Pharmacol Ther 57:552

why: One cigarette raises striatal dopamine only modestly, much less than cocaine or amphetamine.
source: Brody et al. 2004 Am J Psychiatry 161:1211; Di Chiara & Imperato 1988 PNAS 85:5274

why: Moderate aerobic exercise raises blood anandamide, a possible contributor to the 'runner's high'.
source: Raichlen et al. 2012 J Exp Biol 215:1331; Sparling et al. 2003 Neuroreport 14:2209; Dietrich & McDaniel 2004 Br J Sports Med 38:536
